Handkerchiefs
HANG-ker-chifs
n. pl. (cloths carried from Paul's body to the sick at Ephesus)
From hand and kerchief, itself from Old French couvrechief, a head covering. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, in Luke's account of the special miracles God wrought by the hands of Paul at Ephesus.

Biblical Definition

And God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul: so that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them. Luke is careful with the grammar, and the care is doctrine. God wrought, by the hands of Paul, and the miracles are called special — literally, not the ordinary sort — which means Luke himself flags them as exceptional rather than exemplary. The account continues immediately into its own commentary. Certain vagabond Jews, exorcists, tried to use the name as a technique, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth, and the evil spirit answered, Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye? and the man leapt on them and overcame them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. The name is not a formula. The chapter ends where Luke wants it: fear fell on them all, the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified, many burned their books of curious arts, and so mightily grew the word of God and prevailed. The cloths were a sign; the growing word was the result.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a piece of cloth carried about the person for wiping the face; in Scripture, cloths from Paul's body by which God wrought special miracles at Ephesus.

expand to see more

HANDKERCHIEF, n. A piece of cloth, usually silk or linen, carried about the person for wiping the face.

APRON, n. A cloth or piece of leather worn on the fore part of the body, to keep the clothes clean.

MIRACLE, n. In theology, an effect above human or natural power, performed in attestation of some truth.

EXORCIST, n. One who pretends to expel evil spirits by conjuration, prayers and ceremonies.

SUPERSTITION, n. Excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; belief in the direct agency of superior powers in extraordinary events.

Key Scripture

Act 19:12 — "So that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them."

Act 19:13 — "Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth."

Act 19:19 — "Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver."

Act 19:20 — "So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed."

Modern Corruption

The handkerchiefs of Acts 19 are turned into a method — anointed cloths sold or mailed as vehicles of healing — when Luke calls the miracles special and follows them immediately with the story of men who tried to use the name as a technique and were beaten for it.

expand to see more

The prayer-cloth industry rests on this verse and the chapter refutes it in the next breath. Luke marks the miracles as not-the-ordinary-kind, and then narrates what happens when men treat spiritual power as a portable method: the sons of Sceva are stripped and wounded by the very spirit they tried to command. Between those two paragraphs lies the whole difference between God working sovereignly through an apostle to attest the gospel at a pagan capital, and a technique sold to the desperate. The cloths healed because God wrought; nothing is said about the cloths having anything in them.

The city's response shows what the miracles were for. Ephesus was a centre of curious arts, and the men who had practised them brought their books together and burned them publicly at a cost of fifty thousand pieces of silver — not sold, burned, because the money was not the point and the books were not to circulate. That is what an encounter with the true power does to the occult trade. The dictionary holds the cessationist position on the sign-gifts with the Reformed tradition, and this chapter is one of the reasons: the signs attested the apostles, and the apostolic office closed with them, and what remains and grows is the word.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek soudarion (G4676), a napkin or handkerchief; simikinthion (G4612), an apron; dunamis (G1411), power, and so a mighty work.

expand to see more

Greek soudarion (G4676) — a face-cloth, a napkin; also the napkin about the Lord's head in the tomb.

Greek simikinthion (G4612) — a workman's apron; the other cloth named at Ephesus.

Greek dunamis (G1411) — power, a mighty work; God wrought special miracles.

Greek tuchon (from G5177) — ordinary, common; the word Luke negates in calling them special.

Greek horkizo (G3726) — to adjure, to bind by an oath; We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.

Usage

"“from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons” — the single occurrence."

"“Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?” — the answer to the name used as technique."

"“So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed” — the outcome Luke records."
